text:
A simple pendulum of string length 30 cm performs 20 oscillations in 10 s . The length of the string required for the pendulum to perform 40 oscillations in the same time duration is

$____$ cm . [Assume that the mass of the pendulum remains same.]
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 23rd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The time period (T) of a simple pendulum is the time taken to complete one full oscillation.

For a simple pendulum of the length of the string $(\mathrm{L})$ and the acceleration due to gravity $(\mathrm{g})$ the formula for the time period is,

$\mathrm{T}=2π\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{L}}{\mathrm{g}}}$

So, the time period is directly proportional to the square root of the length $(T\propto \sqrt{L})$.

$\mathrm{T}^{2}\propto \mathrm{L}\Rightarrow \propto \mathrm{T}^{2}$

Case - 1

The initial length of the string is $\mathrm{L}_{1}=30\mathrm{cm}$

$\mathrm{N}_{1}=20$ is the number of oscillations completed in total time $\mathrm{t}_{1}=10\mathrm{s}$

So, the initial time period of oscillation is

$\mathrm{T}_{1}=\frac{\text{Total Time}}{\text{Number of Oscillations}}=\frac{10}{20}=0.5\mathrm{s}$

Case - 2

$\mathrm{N}_{2}=40$ is the number of oscillations completed in the same time $\mathrm{t}_{2}=\mathrm{t}_{1}=10\mathrm{s}$

So, the final time period of oscillation is,

$\mathrm{T}_{2}=\frac{\text{Total Time}}{\text{Number of Oscillations}}=\frac{10}{40}=0.25\mathrm{s}$

We need to find the required length $(\mathrm{L}_{2})$ corresponding to the final length of the string, Using the proportionality $\mathrm{L}\propto \mathrm{T}^{2}$

$\frac{\mathrm{L}_{2}}{\mathrm{L}_{1}}=\left (\frac{\mathrm{T}_{2}}{\mathrm{T}_{1}}\right )^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{\mathrm{L}_{2}}{30}=\left (\frac{0.25}{0.50}\right )^{2}=\frac{1}{4}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{\mathrm{L}_{2}}{30}=\frac{1}{4}\Rightarrow \mathrm{L}_{2}=\frac{30}{4}\mathrm{cm}=7.5\mathrm{cm}$

Therefore, the required length of the string is 7.5 cm . 

Hence, the correct option is (B).

text: The de Broglie wavelength of an oxygen molecule at $27^{\circ }\mathrm{C}$ is $x\times 10^{-12}\mathrm{m}$. The value of $x$ is (take Planck's constant $=6.63\times 10^{-34}\mathrm{J}.\mathrm{s}$, Boltzmann constant $=1.38\times 10^{-23}\mathrm{J}/\mathrm{K}$, mass of oxygen molecule $=5.31\times 10^{-26}\mathrm{kg}$ )
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 23rd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Only translational motion gives a molecule linear momentum, so the kinetic energy that fixes $p$ is the translational part $\dfrac{3}{2}k_{B}T$; the rotational energy of the diatomic $\mathrm{O}{}_{2}$ molecule adds no linear momentum.

$p=\sqrt{2m\times \dfrac{3}{2}k_{B}T}=\sqrt{3mk_{B}T}$

With $T=27+273=300\text{K}$:

$3mk_{B}T=3\times 5.31\times 10^{-26}\times 1.38\times 10^{-23}\times 300=6.595\times 10^{-46}$

$p=\sqrt{6.595\times 10^{-46}}=2.568\times 10^{-23}\text{kg m s}^{-1}$

$λ=\dfrac{h}{p}=\dfrac{6.63\times 10^{-34}}{2.568\times 10^{-23}}=2.58\times 10^{-11}\text{m}\approx 26\times 10^{-12}\text{m}$

So $x\approx 26$.

Hence, the correct option is (D).

The strain-stress plot for materials $A,B,C$ and $D$ is shown in the figure. Which material has the largest Young's modulus ?


[IMG]
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 23rd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Young's Modulus (Y) is defined as the ratio of Stress $(σ)$ to Strain $(ε)$ within the elastic limit :

$Y=\frac{\text{Stress}}{\text{Strain}}$

For the given graph,

1. Y -axis: $\mathrm{Strain}(ε)$

2. X -axis: Stress $(σ)$

Since Strain is on the Y -axis and Stress is on the X -axis, the slope of the line is given by :

$\text{Slope}=\frac{\Delta \mathrm{Y}}{\Delta \mathrm{X}}=\frac{\text{Strain}}{\text{Stress}}$

$\text{Slope}=\frac{1}{\mathrm{Y}}$

It shows that the slope is inversely proportional to Young's Modulus, i.e., higher slope corresponds to smaller Young's Modulus (material is more elastic) whereas lower slope shows larger Young's Modulus (material is less elastic).

So, the material with the largest Young's modulus will be the line with the smallest slope.

1. Material A has the highest slope → smallest Y.

2. Material C has the lowest slope → largest Y.

Therefore, material C has the largest Young's modulus. Hence, the correct option is (D).

The following diagram shows a Zener diode as a voltage regulator. The Zener diode is rated at $V_{z}=5\mathrm{V}$ and the desired current in load is 5 mA . The unregulated voltage source can supply upto 25 V . Considering the Zener diode can withstand four times of the load current, the value of resistor $R_{s}$ (shown in circuit) should be $____$ $\Omega$.


[IMG]
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 23rd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The Zener current must not exceed $I_{Z,\max }=4I_{L}=4\times 5\text{mA}=20\text{mA}$. At the highest input voltage with the load disconnected, the whole current through $R_{s}$ passes through the diode, so

$R_{s}=\dfrac{V_{in,\max }-V_{Z}}{I_{Z,\max }}=\dfrac{25-5}{20\times 10^{-3}}=1000\Omega$

With the load connected, the same $20\text{mA}$ divides into $I_{L}=5\text{mA}$ and $I_{Z}=15\text{mA}$, so the diode still holds the output at $5\text{V}$.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

text: A 20 m long uniform copper wire held horizontally is allowed to fall under the gravity $\left (g=10\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}\right )$ through a uniform horizontal magnetic field of 0.5 Gauss perpendicular to the length of the wire. The induced EMF across the wire when it travels a vertical distance of 200 m is $____$ mV .
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 23rd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
When a straight wire falls through a magnetic field, an EMF gets induced across its ends. This is the motional EMF, and it is given by

$ε=Bvl$

where $B$ is the magnetic field, $v$ is the speed of the wire, and $l$ is its length.

Here the wire is falling freely, so first we need its speed after falling through 200 m. Using the equation of motion with initial velocity zero,

$v^{2}=2gh=2\times 10\times 200=4000$

$v=\sqrt{4000}=20\sqrt{10}\text{m/s}$

Now, the magnetic field is given in Gauss, so we convert it to SI units. Since $1$ Gauss $=10^{-4}$ T,

$B=0.5\text{Gauss}=0.5\times 10^{-4}\text{T}$

The wire is horizontal, the field is horizontal and perpendicular to the wire, and the motion is vertical. So $B$, $v$ and $l$ are all mutually perpendicular, and we can directly use $ε=Bvl$.

$ε=0.5\times 10^{-4}\times 20\sqrt{10}\times 20$

$ε=0.5\times 10^{-4}\times 400\sqrt{10}=200\sqrt{10}\times 10^{-4}\text{V}$

$ε=0.02\sqrt{10}\text{V}=20\sqrt{10}\text{mV}$

So the induced EMF across the wire is $20\sqrt{10}$ mV, which is Option C.

Relation

Law

  

  

    A.

    $\int ⃗{E}\cdot \vec{dl}=-\frac{d}{dt}\int ⃗{B}\cdot \vec{da}$

    I.

    Ampere's circuital law

  

  

    B.

    $\int ⃗{B}\cdot \vec{dl}=μ_{0}\left (I+𝜖_{0}\frac{d𝜙_{E}}{dt}\right )$

    II.

    Faraday's laws of electromagnetic induction

  

  

    C.

    $\int ⃗{E}\cdot \vec{da}=\frac{1}{𝜖_{0}}\int _{\mathrm{v}}ρ\mathrm{dv}$

    III.

    Ampere - Maxwell law

  

  

    D.

    $\int ⃗{B}\cdot \vec{dl}=μ_{0}I$

    IV.

    Gauss's law of electrostatics

  

Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 23rd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
For relation A

The equation $\int ⃗{E}\cdot d⃗{l}=-\frac{d}{dt}[\int ⃗{B}\cdot d⃗{a}]$ mathematically states that the line integral of the electric field around a closed loop is equal to the negative rate of change of magnetic flux through the loop. This is the integral form of Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction, i.e., $\mathrm{A}\to$ II

For relation B

This equation $\int \vec{\mathrm{B}}\cdot \mathrm{d}\vec{\mathrm{l}}=μ_{0}\left (\mathrm{I}+𝜖_{0}\frac{\mathrm{d}\Phi _{\mathrm{E}}}{\mathrm{dt}}\right )$ relates the magnetic field line integral to both the conduction current (I) and the displacement current $\left (𝜖_{0}\frac{\mathrm{d}\Phi _{\mathrm{E}}}{\mathrm{dt}}\right )$. This modification to Ampere's Law was introduced by Maxwell to account for changing electric fields. This is the Ampere-Maxwell Law, i.e., $\mathrm{B}\to$ III

For relation C

In relation $C,\int ⃗{E}\cdot d⃗{a}=\frac{1}{𝜖_{0}}\int _{V}ρdV$ the total charge $Q_{\text{enclosed}}$ is represented as $\int ⃗{E}\cdot d⃗{a}$. The equation states that the total electric flux through a closed surface is equal to the enclosed charge divided by $𝜖_{0}$. This is Gauss's Law of Electrostatics, i.e., $\mathrm{C}\to$ IV

For relation D

This relation $\int \vec{\mathrm{B}}\cdot d\vec{\mathrm{l}}=μ_{0}\mathrm{I}$ states that the line integral of the magnetic field around a closed loop is equal to $μ_{0}$ times the current enclosed by the loop. This is the original form of Ampere's Circuital Law which is valid for steady currents, i.e., $\mathrm{D}\to \mathrm{I}$

So, the correct match is $\mathrm{A}\to$ II, $\mathrm{B}\to$ III, $\mathrm{C}\to$ IV, $\mathrm{D}\to$ I. Hence, the correct option is (B).

text: Two small balls with masses $m$ and 2 m are attached to both ends of a rigid rod of length $d$ and negligible mass. If angular momentum of this system is $L$ about an axis (A) passing through its centre of mass and perpendicular to the rod then angular velocity of the system about $A$ is :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 23rd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Let the mass m be at position $\mathrm{x}=0$.

The mass 2 m is at position $\mathrm{x}=\mathrm{d}$.


[IMG]


The position of the centre of mass $(\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{CM}})$ is given by :

$\mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{CM}}=\frac{\mathrm{m}_{1}\mathrm{x}_{1}+\mathrm{m}_{2}\mathrm{x}_{2}}{\mathrm{m}_{1}+\mathrm{m}_{2}}$

$X_{CM}=\frac{m(0)+2m(d)}{m+2m}=\frac{2md}{3m}=\frac{2d}{3}$

So, the distances of the masses from the centre of mass are :

Distance of mass m from $\mathrm{CM}(\mathrm{r}_{1})$ :

$r_{1}=\frac{2d}{3}$

Distance of mass 2 m from CM ( $\mathrm{r}_{2}$ ) :

$\mathrm{r}_{2}=\mathrm{d}-\frac{2\mathrm{d}}{3}=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{3}$

The moment of inertia of the system about the axis passing through the CM is the sum of the moments of inertia of the individual masses :

$\mathrm{I}=\mathrm{m}_{1}\mathrm{r}_{1}^{2}+\mathrm{m}_{2}\mathrm{r}_{2}^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $I=m\left (\frac{2d}{3}\right )^{2}+2m\left (\frac{d}{3}\right )^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $I=m\left (\frac{4d^{2}}{9}\right )+2m\left (\frac{d^{2}}{9}\right )$

$\Rightarrow$ $I=\frac{4\mathrm{md}^{2}}{9}+\frac{2\mathrm{md}^{2}}{9}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{I}=\frac{6\mathrm{md}^{2}}{9}=\frac{2}{3}\mathrm{md}^{2}$

The angular momentum L is related to the moment of inertia I and angular velocity $ω$ by the formula:

$\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{I}ω$

$\Rightarrow ω=\frac{L}{I}=\frac{L}{\left (\frac{2}{3}\mathrm{md}^{2}\right )}$

$\Rightarrow ω=\frac{3}{2}\frac{\mathrm{L}}{\mathrm{md}^{2}}$

Therefore, the angular velocity of the system is $\frac{3}{2}\frac{\mathrm{L}}{\mathrm{md}^{2}}$. 

Hence, the correct option is (B).

text:
An object is projected with kinetic energy $K$ from a point $A$ at an angle $60^{\circ }$ with the horizontal. The ratio of the difference in kinetic energies at points $B$ and $C$ to that at point $A$ (see figure), in the absence of air friction is :


[IMG]
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 23rd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Let the mass of the object be m and the initial speed be u .

The angle of projection is $θ=60^{\circ }$.

At point A

The kinetic energy at point $A$ is given as $K$.

$\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{A}}=\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{mu}^{2}=\mathrm{K}$

At Point B (Maximum Height)

At the highest point of a projectile's path, the vertical component of velocity becomes zero $(v_{y}=0)$. The object only possesses the horizontal component of velocity ( $\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{x}}$ ).

The horizontal velocity remains constant throughout the motion (assuming no air resistance):

$\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{B}}=\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{x}}=\mathrm{u}\cos θ$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{B}}=\mathrm{u}\cos 60^{\circ }=\mathrm{u}\left (\frac{1}{2}\right )=\frac{\mathrm{u}}{2}$

So, the kinetic energy at B is,

$\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{B}}=\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{m}(\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{B}})^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{B}}=\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{m}\left (\frac{\mathrm{u}}{2}\right )^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{B}}=\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{m}\left (\frac{\mathrm{u}^{2}}{4}\right )$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{B}}=\frac{1}{4}\left (\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{mu}^{2}\right )=\frac{1}{4}\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{A}}=\frac{\mathrm{K}}{4}$

$\Rightarrow \mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{B}}=\frac{\mathrm{K}}{4}$

At Point C

Point C is at the same horizontal level as point A . By the law of conservation of energy, the speed of the projectile when it hits the ground at the same level is equal to the speed of projection.

$\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{C}}=\mathrm{u}$

Therefore, the kinetic energy at C is equal to the kinetic energy at A :

$\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{C}}=\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{A}}=\mathrm{K}$

The difference in kinetic energies at B and C :

$\Delta K_{BC}=|K_{C}-K_{B}|=\left |K-\frac{K}{4}\right |=\frac{3K}{4}$

So, the ratio of the difference in kinetic energies at points B and C to that at point A is

Ratio $=\frac{\Delta K_{BC}}{K_{A}}=\frac{(3/4)K}{K}=\frac{3}{4}$

Hence, the correct option is (A).

text:
In a perfectly inelastic collision, two spheres made of the same material with masses 15 kg and 25 kg , moving in opposite directions with speeds of $10\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}$ and $30\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}$, respectively, strike each other and stick together. The rise in temperature (in ${}^{\circ }\mathrm{C}$ ), if all the heat produced during the collision is retained by these spheres, is :

(specific heat of sphere material $31\mathrm{cal}/\mathrm{kg}.{}^{\circ }\mathrm{C}$ and $1\mathrm{cal}=4.2\mathrm{J}$ )
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 23rd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Before Collision :


[IMG]


The masses of the spheres are, $\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{A}}=15\mathrm{kg},\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{B}}=25\mathrm{kg}$

The initial velocities of the spheres are, $\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{A}}=10\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s},\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{B}}=-30\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}$

Hence, the kinetic energy of system before collision is,

$\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{i}}=\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{A}}\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{A}}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{B}}\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{B}}^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{i}}=\frac{1}{2}(15)(10)^{2}+\frac{1}{2}(25)(30)^{2}=750+11250=12000\mathrm{J}$

Since the collision is perfectly inelastic, the spheres stick together and move with a common final velocity $\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{f}}$.


[IMG]


Using conservation of linear momentum,

$m_{A}u_{A}+m_{B}u_{B}=(m_{A}+m_{B})v_{f}$

$\Rightarrow$ $(15)(10)+(25)(-30)=(15+25)v_{f}$

$\Rightarrow$ $150-750=40v_{f}$

$-600=40v_{f}\Rightarrow v_{f}=-15\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}$

(The negative sign indicates the combined mass moves in the direction of the 25 kg sphere.)

So, the final kinetic energy of the system is

$\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{f}}=\frac{1}{2}(\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{A}}+\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{B}})\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{f}}^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{f}}=\frac{1}{2}(40)(15)^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{f}}=4500\mathrm{J}$

The loss in kinetic energy appears as heat (Q).

$Q=K_{i}-K_{f}$

$\Rightarrow$ $Q=12000\mathrm{J}-4500\mathrm{J}$

$Q=7500\mathrm{J}$

Using the heat capacity formula $\mathrm{Q}=\mathrm{mc}\Delta \mathrm{T}$.

Where, total mass (m) of the spheres is 40 kg , the specific heat (c) of the material of spheres is $31\mathrm{cal}/\mathrm{kg}\cdot {}^{\circ }\mathrm{C}$.

As $1\mathrm{cal}=4.2\mathrm{J}$, so $\mathrm{c}=31\times 4.2\mathrm{J}/\mathrm{kg}\cdot {}^{\circ }\mathrm{C}=130.2\mathrm{J}/\mathrm{kg}\cdot {}^{\circ }\mathrm{C}$

Substituting the values in heat capacity formula,

$7500=40\times 130.2\times \Delta \mathrm{T}$

$\Rightarrow$ $7500=5208\times \Delta \mathrm{T}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\Delta \mathrm{T}=\frac{7500}{5208}\approx 1.44^{\circ }\mathrm{C}$

Therefore, the rise in temperature is $1.44^{\circ }\mathrm{C}$. 

Hence, the correct option is (B).

text:
In hydrogen atom spectrum, ( $R\to$ Rydberg's constant)

A. the maximum wavelength of the radiation of Lyman series is $\frac{4}{3R}$

B. the Balmer series lies in the visible region of the spectrum

C. the minimum wavelength of the radiation of Paschen series is $\frac{9}{R}$

D. the minimum wavelength of Lyman series is $\frac{5}{4R}$

Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 23rd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
For hydrogen, $\dfrac{1}{λ}=R\left (\dfrac{1}{n_{1}^{2}}-\dfrac{1}{n_{2}^{2}}\right )$; the longest wavelength of a series comes from $n_{2}=n_{1}+1$ and the shortest from $n_{2}=\infty$.

Statement A: for Lyman ($n_{1}=1$), the longest wavelength is from $n_{2}=2$: $\dfrac{1}{λ_{\max }}=R\left (1-\dfrac{1}{4}\right )=\dfrac{3R}{4}\Rightarrow λ_{\max }=\dfrac{4}{3R}$. Correct.

Statement B: Balmer lines ($n_{2}\geq 3\to n_{1}=2$), such as $656\text{nm}$, $486\text{nm}$, $434\text{nm}$ and $410\text{nm}$, lie in the visible region. Correct.

Statement C: for Paschen ($n_{1}=3$), the shortest wavelength is from $n_{2}=\infty$: $\dfrac{1}{λ_{\min }}=\dfrac{R}{9}\Rightarrow λ_{\min }=\dfrac{9}{R}$. Correct.

Statement D: for Lyman, the shortest wavelength is from $n_{2}=\infty$: $\dfrac{1}{λ_{\min }}=R\Rightarrow λ_{\min }=\dfrac{1}{R}$, not $\dfrac{5}{4R}$. Incorrect.

Statements A, B and C are correct.

Hence, the correct option is (D).

text:
Two point charges $2q$ and $q$ are placed at vertex $A$ and centre of face $CDEF$ of the cube as shown in figure. The electric flux passing through the cube is:


[IMG]
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 23rd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
According to Gauss's Law, the total electric flux $\Phi$ through a closed surface is

$\Phi =\frac{Q_{\text{enclosed}}}{𝜖_{0}}$

For the flux contribution from charge at vertex $\mathrm{A}(2\mathrm{q})$

As the charge 2 q is placed at a corner (vertex) of the cube.

A corner of a cube is a meeting point for 8 identical cubes stacked together


[IMG]


Since the charge is shared equally among 8 cubes, the portion of the flux entering the specific cube is $\frac{1}{8}$ of the total flux produced by the charge.

$\Phi _{\mathrm{A}}=\frac{1}{8}\times \frac{2\mathrm{q}}{𝜖_{0}}=\frac{2\mathrm{q}}{8𝜖_{0}}=\frac{\mathrm{q}}{4𝜖_{0}}$

For the flux contribution from charge at the centre of face CDEF (q)

The charge q is placed at the center of the face CDEF and a face of a cube is shared by exactly 2 identical cubes placed side-by-side.


[IMG]


Since the charge is shared equally between 2 cubes, the portion of the flux entering the specific cube is $\frac{1}{2}$ of the total flux produced by the charge.

$\Phi _{\text{face}}=\frac{1}{2}\times \frac{q}{𝜖_{0}}=\frac{q}{2𝜖_{0}}$

The total flux passing through the cube is the sum of the contributions from both charges.

$\Phi _{\text{total}}=\Phi _{\mathrm{A}}+\Phi _{\text{face}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\Phi _{\text{total}}=\frac{\mathrm{q}}{4𝜖_{0}}+\frac{\mathrm{q}}{2𝜖_{0}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\Phi _{\text{total}}=\frac{q+2q}{4𝜖_{0}}=\frac{3q}{4𝜖_{0}}$

Therefore, the total electric flux passing through the cube is $\frac{3q}{4𝜖_{0}}$. 

Hence, the correct option is (B).

text: The moment of inertia of a square loop made of four uniform solid cylinders, each having radius $R$ and length $L(\mathrm{R}<\mathrm{L})$ about an axis passing through the mid points of opposite sides, is (Take the mass of the entire loop as $M$ ) :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 23rd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
[IMG]


Total mass of the square loop is M which is made of 4 identical solid cylinders.

So, mass of each cylinder $=m=\frac{M}{4}$

The length of each cylinder is L and radius is R .

Axis of rotation passes through the midpoints of two opposite sides.

Let's assume the square lies in the xy -plane and the axis bisects the square vertically.

For the cylinder B and D

The axis passes through the center of these cylinders and is perpendicular to their length.

The Moment of Inertia ( $\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{B}},\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{D}}$ ) of a solid cylinder about a transverse axis passing through its center is:

$\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{B}}=\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{D}}=\frac{\mathrm{mL}^{2}}{12}+\frac{\mathrm{mR}^{2}}{4}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{B}}+\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{D}}=2\left (\frac{\mathrm{mL}^{2}}{12}+\frac{\mathrm{mR}^{2}}{4}\right )=\left (\frac{\mathrm{mL}^{2}}{6}+\frac{\mathrm{mR}^{2}}{2}\right )$

For the cylinders A and C :

The axis is parallel to the length of these cylinders.

The axis is at a distance $\mathrm{d}=\frac{\mathrm{L}}{2}$ from the center of each cylinder.

The Moment of Inertia ( $\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{CM}}$ ) of a solid cylinder about its own longitudinal axis is $\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{mR}^{2}$.

Using the Parallel Axis Theorem ( $\mathrm{I}=\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{CM}}+\mathrm{md}^{2}$ ), the inertia of one such cylinder about the central axis is:

$\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{A}}=\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{C}}=\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{mR}^{2}+\mathrm{m}\left (\frac{\mathrm{L}}{2}\right )^{2}=\frac{\mathrm{mR}^{2}}{2}+\frac{\mathrm{mL}^{2}}{4}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{A}}+\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{C}}=2\times \left (\frac{\mathrm{mR}^{2}}{2}+\frac{\mathrm{mL}^{2}}{4}\right )=\left (\mathrm{mR}^{2}+\frac{\mathrm{mL}^{2}}{2}\right )$

Hence, the total moment of inertia of system about the given axis of rotation is,

$\mathrm{I}_{\text{total}}=\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{A}}+\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{B}}+\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{C}}+\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{D}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{I}_{\text{total}}=\left (\frac{\mathrm{mL}^{2}}{6}+\frac{\mathrm{mR}^{2}}{2}\right )+\left (\mathrm{mR}^{2}+\frac{\mathrm{mL}^{2}}{2}\right )$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{I}_{\text{total}}=\left (\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{2}\right )\mathrm{mL}^{2}+\left (\frac{1}{2}+1\right )\mathrm{mR}^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{I}_{\text{total}}=\frac{4}{6}\mathrm{mL}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}\mathrm{mR}^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{I}_{\text{total}}=\frac{2}{3}\mathrm{mL}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}\mathrm{mR}^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{I}_{\text{total}}=\frac{2}{3}\left (\frac{\mathrm{M}}{4}\right )\mathrm{L}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}\left (\frac{\mathrm{M}}{4}\right )\mathrm{R}^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{I}_{\text{total}}=\frac{2}{12}\mathrm{ML}^{2}+\frac{3}{8}\mathrm{MR}^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{I}_{\text{total}}=\frac{1}{6}\mathrm{ML}^{2}+\frac{3}{8}\mathrm{MR}^{2}$

Hence, the correct option is (D).

text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Consider a ferromagnetic material :

Assertion (A) : The individual atoms in a ferromagnetic material possess a magnetic dipole moment and interact with one another in such a way that they spontaneously align themselves forming domains.

Reason (R) : At high enough temperature, the domain structure of ferromagnetic material disintegrates. Thus, magnetization will disappear at high enough temperature known as Curie temperature.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below :
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 23rd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Ferromagnetic materials (like iron, nickel, cobalt) are characterized by the fact that their individual atoms possess a permanent magnetic dipole moment. Due to strong quantum mechanical interactions between neighbouring atoms, these dipoles spontaneously align parallel to each other within small macroscopic regions.

These aligned regions are indeed called magnetic domains. Within a domain, the magnetization is saturated, even in the absence of an external field.


[IMG]


Hence, the Assertion (A) is True.

Temperature represents thermal agitation. As the temperature of a ferromagnetic material increases, the thermal energy tends to randomize the orientation of the magnetic dipoles.

At a specific critical temperature called the Curie Temperature ( $\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{c}}$ ), the thermal agitation becomes strong enough to overcome the exchange coupling that holds the domains together. The domain structure breaks down (disintegrates), and the material transitions from ferromagnetic to paramagnetic, losing its spontaneous magnetization.

So, the Reason (R) is also True.

The formation of domains (A) is caused by the minimization of exchange energy and magnetostatic energy. The destruction of domains at high temperature ( R ) is a property of the material's phase transition.

Knowing that domains disappear at high heat does not explain the fundamental physical mechanism (exchange interaction) that causes them to align spontaneously at lower temperatures.

Both statements are correct facts, but R is not the functional explanation for A , i.e., both $(\mathrm{A})$ and $(\mathrm{R})$ are true but $(\mathrm{R})$ is not the correct explanation of (A). 

Hence, the correct option is (D).

A small bob $A$ of mass $m$ is attached to a massless rigid rod of length 1 m pivoted at point $P$ and kept at an angle of $60^{\circ }$ with vertical as shown in figure. At distance of 1 m below point $P$, an identical bob $B$ is kept at rest on a smooth horizontal surface that extends to a circular track of radius $R$ as shown in figure. If bob $B$ just manages to complete the circular path of radius $R$ upto a point $Q$ after being hit elastically by $\mathrm{bob}A$, then radius $R$ is $____$ m.


[IMG]
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 23rd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Bob A is released from rest at an angle $θ=60^{\circ }$. It swings down to the lowest point (vertical position) where it hits Bob B.

Length of rod is $\mathrm{l}=1\mathrm{m}$.

Height lost by $\mathrm{A}(\Delta \mathrm{h})$ :


[IMG]


$\Delta \mathrm{h}=\mathrm{l}-\mathrm{l}\cos θ=\mathrm{l}(1-\cos 60^{\circ })$

$\Rightarrow$ $\Delta \mathrm{h}=1(1-0.5)=0.5\mathrm{m}$

Using conservation of energy for Bob A :

$\mathrm{mg}\Delta \mathrm{h}=\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{A}}^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{A}}=\sqrt{2\mathrm{g}\Delta \mathrm{h}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{A}}=\sqrt{2\mathrm{g}\times 0.5}=\sqrt{\mathrm{g}}$

It is given that the collision is elastic. Both bobs are identical (mass m ).

Initial velocities: $\mathrm{Bob}A$ has $v_{A}=\sqrt{g}$, $\mathrm{Bob}B$ is at rest $(v_{B}=0)$.

In a perfectly elastic collision between two identical masses where one is initially at rest, their velocities are exchanged.

So, after collision, bob A comes to rest and bob B acquires the velocity of Bob A .

$\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{B}}=\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{A}}=\sqrt{\mathrm{g}}$

Bob B moves along the smooth horizontal surface and enters the vertical circular track of radius R.

The bob B just manages to complete the circular path up to a point Q .

For a particle to just complete a full vertical circle (reach the top), the minimum velocity at the bottom $(\sqrt{5\mathrm{gR}})$ is required.

$\mathrm{v}_{\text{bottom}}\geq \sqrt{5\mathrm{gR}}$

$\Rightarrow \sqrt{g}=\sqrt{5gR}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\Rightarrow \mathrm{g}=5\mathrm{gR}$

$\Rightarrow \mathrm{R}=\frac{1}{5}\mathrm{m}$

Therefore, the required radius $R$ is $\frac{1}{5}\mathrm{m}$. Hence, the correct option is (A).

text: A thin prism with angle $5^{\circ }$ of refractive index 1.72 is combined with another prism of refractive index 1.9 to produce dispersion without deviation. The angle of second prism is $____$ .
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 23rd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
When two thin prisms are combined to produce dispersion without deviation, they are arranged such that their refracting angles are inverted relative to each other. The net deviation produced by the combination is zero.


[IMG]


$δ_{\text{net}}=δ_{1}-δ_{2}=0$

$\Rightarrow$ $δ_{1}=δ_{2}$

The deviation $(δ)$ produced by a thin prism is given by the formula :

$δ=(μ-1)\mathrm{A}$

where :

$μ$ is the refractive index of the material.

A is the angle of the prism.

Since the deviations must be equal and opposite :

$(μ_{1}-1)\mathrm{A}_{1}=(μ_{2}-1)\mathrm{A}_{2}$

The angle of prism for first prism is $\mathrm{A}_{1}=5^{\circ }$ and its refractive index is $μ_{1}=1.72$

The refractive index of the second prism is $μ_{2}=1.9$

$(1.72-1)\times 5^{\circ }=(1.9-1)\times \mathrm{A}_{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $3.6=0.9\times \mathrm{A}_{2}\Rightarrow \mathrm{A}_{2}=\frac{3.6}{0.9}=4^{\circ }$

Therefore, the angle of the second prism is $4^{\circ }$. Hence, the correct option is (B).

text:
A wire of uniform resistance $λ\Omega /\mathrm{m}$ is bent into a circle of radius $r$ and another piece of wire with length $2r$ is connected between points $A$ and $B(\mathrm{AOB})$ as shown in figure. The equivalent resistance between points $A$ and $B$ is $____$ $\Omega$.


[IMG]
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 23rd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
For the equivalent resistance between points A and B we can identify three distinct paths for the current to flow from node A to node B. These paths are in parallel.


[IMG]



[IMG]


The resistance per unit length for the wire is $λ\Omega /\mathrm{m}$

The resistance is given by $\mathrm{R}=$ Resistance per unit length × Length $=λ\times \mathrm{L}$.

Path 1 (Minor Arc AB):

The shorter curved wire along the circle's circumference. Since $\angle \mathrm{AOB}=90^{\circ }$ (a quarter circle), the length is $\frac{1}{4}$ of the circumference.

$\mathrm{L}_{1}=\frac{1}{4}\times 2π\mathrm{r}=\frac{π\mathrm{r}}{2}$

So, the resistance of path 1 is,

$\mathrm{R}_{1}=λ\left (\frac{π\mathrm{r}}{2}\right )$

Path 2 (Major Arc AOB):

The longer curved wire along the remaining part of the circle. This is $\frac{3}{4}$ of the circumference.

$\mathrm{L}_{2}=\frac{3}{4}\times 2π\mathrm{r}=\frac{3π\mathrm{r}}{2}$

So, the resistance of path 2 is,

$\mathrm{R}_{2}=λ\left (\frac{3π\mathrm{r}}{2}\right )$

Path 3 (Wire AOB):

The straight wire sections connecting A to the centre O and then O to B . Thus, the two segments AO and OB are in series. It is given that the length of this wire is $2r$.

$\mathrm{L}_{3}=\mathrm{r}+\mathrm{r}=2\mathrm{r}$

So, the resistance of path 3 is,

$\mathrm{R}_{34}=\mathrm{R}_{3}+\mathrm{R}_{4}=λ(2\mathrm{r})$

Since the three paths are in parallel, the equivalent resistance $(R_{eq})$ is,

$\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{eq}}}=\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}_{1}}+\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}_{2}}+\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}_{34}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{1}{R_{eq}}=\frac{1}{λπr/2}+\frac{1}{3λπr/2}+\frac{1}{2λr}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{1}{R_{eq}}=\frac{2}{λπr}+\frac{2}{3λπr}+\frac{1}{2λr}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{eq}}}=\frac{1}{λ\mathrm{r}}\left [\frac{2}{π}+\frac{2}{3π}+\frac{1}{2}\right ]$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{eq}}}=\frac{1}{λ\mathrm{r}}\left [\frac{12+4+3π}{6π}\right ]$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{eq}}}=\frac{1}{λ\mathrm{r}}\left [\frac{16+3π}{6π}\right ]$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{eq}}=λ\mathrm{r}\left [\frac{6π}{16+3π}\right ]=\frac{6λπ\mathrm{r}}{3π+16}$

Therefore, the equivalent resistance between points A and B is $\frac{6λπ\mathrm{r}}{3π+16}$. 

Hence, the correct option is (B).

Two blocks with masses 100 g and 200 g are attached to the ends of springs $A$ and $B$ as shown in figure. The energy stored in $A$ is $E$. The energy stored in $B$, when spring constants $k_{A},k_{B}$ of $A$ and $B$, respectively satisfy the relation $4k_{A}=3k_{B}$, is :


[IMG]
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 23rd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
When a mass $m$ is suspended from a spring of constant $k$, the spring stretches.

If the stretch in spring is $\mathrm{x},\mathrm{kx}=\mathrm{mg}\Rightarrow \mathrm{x}=\frac{\mathrm{mg}}{\mathrm{k}}$

The potential energy ( $U$ ) stored in the spring is given by :

$\mathrm{U}=\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{kx}^{2}$

Substituting $\mathrm{x}=\frac{\mathrm{mg}}{\mathrm{k}}$ :

$\mathrm{U}=\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{k}\left (\frac{\mathrm{mg}}{\mathrm{k}}\right )^{2}=\frac{(\mathrm{mg})^{2}}{2\mathrm{k}}$

Mass of block A is $\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{A}}=100\mathrm{g}$.

The spring constant is $\mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{A}}$.

So, the stored energy in spring A is $\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{A}}=\mathrm{E}$.

Using the formula :

$E=\frac{(m_{A}g)^{2}}{2k_{A}}$

Mass of block B is $\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{B}}=200\mathrm{g}=2\times 100\mathrm{g}=2\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{A}}$

The spring constant of spring B is $\mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{B}}$.

It is given that $4\mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{A}}=3\mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{B}}\Rightarrow \mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{B}}=\frac{4}{3}\mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{A}}$.

So, the stored energy in spring B is

$\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{B}}=\frac{(\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{B}}\mathrm{g})^{2}}{2\mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{B}}}$

Substituting $\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{B}}=2\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{A}}$ and $\mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{B}}=\frac{4}{3}\mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{A}}$ :

$E_{B}=\frac{(2m_{A}g)^{2}}{2\left (\frac{4}{3}k_{A}\right )}$

$\begin{array}{l} \Rightarrow \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{B}}=\dfrac{4\times \frac{3}{8}\times (\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{A}}\mathrm{g})^{2}}{\mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{A}}} \\ \Rightarrow \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{B}}=\dfrac{12}{8}\times \dfrac{(\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{A}}\mathrm{g})^{2}}{\mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{A}}} \\ \Rightarrow \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{B}}=\dfrac{3}{2}\times \dfrac{(\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{A}}\mathrm{g})^{2}}{\mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{A}}} \\ \Rightarrow \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{B}}=3\times \left (\dfrac{(\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{A}}\mathrm{g})^{2}}{2\mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{A}}}\right ) \\ \Rightarrow \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{B}}=3\mathrm{E} \end{array}$

text:
In a screw gauge, the zero of the circular scale lies 3 divisions above the horizontal pitch line when their metallic studs are brought in contact. Using this instrument thickness of a sheet is measured. If pitch scale reading is 1 mm and the circular scale reading is 51 then the correct thickness of the sheet is $____$ mm.

[Assume least count is 0.01 mm ]
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 23rd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The circular scale lies 3 divisions above the horizontal pitch line when the studs are in contact.

When the zero mark is above the reference line, the screw has been turned past the zero point. This indicates a negative zero error. The error corresponds to 3 divisions.

Hence, the zero error is,

$\mathrm{E}_{0}=-(3\times \text{Least Count})=-(3\times 0.01\mathrm{mm})=-0.03\mathrm{mm}$

The observed reading is the sum of the Pitch Scale Reading (PSR) and the Circular Scale Reading (CSR) multiplied by the Least Count (LC).

The given Pitch Scale Reading (PSR) is 1 mm and the Circular Scale Reading (CSR) is 51

So, the observed reading $=\mathrm{PSR}+(\mathrm{CSR}\times \mathrm{LC})$

Observed Reading $=1\mathrm{mm}+(51\times 0.01\mathrm{mm})$

Observed Reading $=1\mathrm{mm}+0.51\mathrm{mm}$

Observed Reading $=1.51\mathrm{mm}$

To find the true thickness, we must subtract the zero error from the observed reading.

Correct Reading $=$ Observed Reading - Zero Error

Correct Reading $=1.51\mathrm{mm}-(-0.03\mathrm{mm})$

Correct Reading $=1.51\mathrm{mm}+0.03\mathrm{mm}$

Correct Reading $=1.54\mathrm{mm}$

Therefore, the correct thickness of the sheet is 1.54 mm. 

Hence, the correct option is (A).

text: Consider light travelling from a medium $A$ to medium $B$ separated by a plane interface. If the light undergoes total internal reflection during its travel from medium $A$ to $B$ and the speed of light in media $A$ and $B$ are $2.4\times 10^{8}\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}$ and $2.7\times 10^{8}\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}$, respectively, then the value of critical angle is :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 23rd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
For total internal reflection to occur, light must travel from a denser medium (lower speed) to a rarer medium (higher speed).

The speed of light in medium A (Denser) is $\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{A}}=2.4\times 10^{8}\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}$

The speed of light in medium $B$ (rarer) is $v_{B}=2.7\times 10^{8}\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}$

Since $\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{A}}<\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{B}}$, medium A is indeed optically denser than medium B , satisfying the condition for TIR.

The critical angle is determined by Snell's Law at the boundary where the angle of refraction is $90^{\circ }$ :

$n_{A}\sin (θ_{c})=n_{B}\sin (90^{\circ })\Rightarrow \sin (θ_{c})=\frac{n_{B}}{n_{A}}$


[IMG]


Since the refractive index n is inversely proportional to the speed of light $\left (\mathrm{n}=\frac{\mathrm{c}}{\mathrm{v}}\right )$,

$\frac{n_{B}}{n_{A}}=\frac{c/v_{B}}{c/v_{A}}=\frac{v_{A}}{v_{B}}$

So,

$\sin (θ_{c})=\frac{v_{A}}{v_{B}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\sin (θ_{C})=\frac{2.4\times 10^{8}}{2.7\times 10^{8}}=\frac{8}{9}$


[IMG]


$\tan (θ_{c})=\frac{8}{\sqrt{9^{2}-8^{2}}}=\frac{8}{\sqrt{17}}\Rightarrow θ_{c}=\tan ^{-1}\left (\frac{8}{\sqrt{17}}\right )$

Therefore, the critical angle is $\tan ^{-1}\left (\frac{8}{\sqrt{17}}\right )$. 

Hence, the correct option is (D).

text: Four persons measure the length of a rod as $20.00\mathrm{cm},19.75\mathrm{cm},17.01\mathrm{cm}$ and 18.25 cm . The relative error in the measurement of average length of the rod is :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 23rd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The average (mean) of the measured values is the true value for our error calculation.

$\bar{x}=\frac{x_{1}+x_{2}+x_{3}+x_{4}}{4}$

Substituting the given values :

$\bar{x}=\frac{20.00+19.75+17.01+18.25}{4}=\frac{75.01}{4}$

$\mathrm{x}–=18.7525\approx 18.75\mathrm{cm}$

The absolute error is the magnitude of the difference between each individual measurement and the mean value.

$|\Delta \mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{i}}|=|\mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{i}}-\mathrm{x}–|$

$\Rightarrow$ $|\Delta \mathrm{x}_{1}|=|20.00-18.75|=1.25$

$\Rightarrow$ $|\Delta \mathrm{x}_{2}|=|19.75-18.75|=1.00$

$\Rightarrow$ $|\Delta x_{3}|=|17.01-18.75|=|-1.74|=1.74$

$\Rightarrow$ $|\Delta \mathrm{x}_{4}|=|18.25-18.75|=|-0.50|=0.50$

Then the average of these absolute errors.

$\Delta \mathrm{x}–=\frac{\sum |\Delta \mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{i}}|}{4}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\Delta \bar{x}=\frac{1.25+1.00+1.74+0.50}{4}=\frac{4.49}{4}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\Delta \mathrm{x}–=1.1225\approx 1.12\mathrm{cm}$

The relative error is defined as the ratio of the mean absolute error to the mean value.

Relative Error $=\frac{\Delta \mathrm{x}–}{\mathrm{x}–}$

Relative Error $=\frac{1.1225}{18.7525}$

Relative Error $\approx 0.0598$

Rounding to two decimal places,

Relative Error $\approx 0.06$

Therefore, the relative error in the measurement is 0.06 . Hence, the correct option is (C).

text:
A simple pendulum made of mass 10 g and a metallic wire of length 10 cm is suspended vertically in a uniform magnetic field of 2 T . The magnetic field direction is perpendicular to the plane of oscillations of the pendulum. If the pendulum is released from an angle of $60^{\circ }$ with vertical, then maximum induced EMF between the point of suspension and point of oscillation is

$____$ mV . (Take $\mathrm{g}=10\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$ )
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 23rd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The mass $(\mathrm{m})$ of the bob is $10\mathrm{g}=0.01\mathrm{kg}$

The length of wire is $\mathrm{l}=10\mathrm{cm}=0.1\mathrm{m}$.

The magnetic field is uniform in the region with strength, $B=2T$.

The pendulum is released from angle $θ=60^{\circ }$

The conducting rod of length 1 rotating around a fixed pivot point with a constant angular velocity $ω$. The rotation takes place in a uniform magnetic field $B$ that is perpendicular to the plane of rotation.

Imagine a small element of length $dr$ on the rod located at a distance $r$ from the pivot point (axis of rotation).


[IMG]


The linear velocity v of this small element is related to the angular velocity $ω$ by the relation:

$\mathrm{v}=\mathrm{r}ω$

The induced EMF ( $\mathrm{d}ε$ ) in a small conductor of length dr moving with velocity v perpendicular to a magnetic field $B$ is given by:

$\mathrm{d}ε=\mathrm{B}\cdot \mathrm{v}\cdot \mathrm{dr}$

However, unlike a rod moving in a straight line, a rotating rod has different velocities at different points. The part near the pivot moves slowly, while the tip moves fastest as $\mathrm{v}=\mathrm{r}ω\Rightarrow \mathrm{v}\propto \mathrm{r}$

To find the total EMF ( $ε$ ) across the entire rod, we integrate the small EMFs from the pivot ( $r=0$ ) to the tip of the $\mathrm{rod}(\mathrm{r}=\mathrm{l})$.

$ε=\int\limits _{0}^{ε}\mathrm{d}ε=\int\limits _{0}^{\mathrm{r}}\mathrm{B}\cdot \mathrm{v}\cdot \mathrm{dr}=\int\limits _{0}^{\mathrm{r}}\mathrm{B}\cdot (ω\mathrm{r})\cdot \mathrm{dr}$

$\Rightarrow$ $ε=\mathrm{B}ω\int\limits _{0}^{1}\mathrm{rdr}$

$\Rightarrow$ $ε=\mathrm{B}ω\left [\frac{\mathrm{r}^{2}}{2}\right ]_{0}^{1}$

$\Rightarrow$ $ε=\mathrm{B}ω\left (\frac{\mathrm{l}^{2}}{2}-\frac{0^{2}}{2}\right )$

$\Rightarrow$ $ε=\mathrm{B}ω\left (\frac{\mathrm{l}^{2}}{2}\right )$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{E}=\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{B}ω\mathrm{l}^{2}$

To find the maximum induced EMF, we need to find the point where the angular velocity $ω$ (and consequently the linear speed v ) is maximum. For a pendulum, the speed is highest at the lowest point of its swing (the equilibrium position).

If the pendulum is released from an angle $θ$, then the lost in height is,


[IMG]


$\mathrm{h}=\mathrm{l}(1-\cos θ)$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{h}=0.1\times (1-\cos 60^{\circ })$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{h}=0.1\times (1-0.5)=0.05\mathrm{m}$

Using Conservation of Energy, when the pendulum is released from an angle $θ$, it loses potential energy and gains kinetic energy as it swings down.

$\mathrm{mg}\Delta \mathrm{h}=\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{v}_{\max }^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{v}_{\max }=\sqrt{2\mathrm{gh}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{v}_{\max }=\sqrt{2\times 10\times 0.05}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{v}_{\max }=\sqrt{1}=1\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}$

Using the relationship between linear velocity (v) and angular velocity ( $ω$ ) is $\mathrm{v}=ω\mathrm{l}$.

$ω_{\max }=\frac{v_{\max }}{l}$

$\Rightarrow$ $ω_{\max }=\frac{1}{0.1}=10\mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}$

Substituting the values into the rotational EMF formula :

$\mathrm{E}_{\max }=\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{B}ω_{\max }\mathrm{l}^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{E}_{\max }=\frac{1}{2}\times 2\times 10\times (0.1)^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{E}_{\max }=1\times 10\times 0.01$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{E}_{\max }=0.1\mathrm{V}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{E}_{\max }=0.1\times 1000\mathrm{mV}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{E}_{\max }=100\mathrm{mV}$

Therefore, the maximum induced EMF is 100 mV . 

Hence, the correct answer is $𝟏 𝟎 𝟎$.

text:
The space between the plates of a parallel plate capacitor of capacitance C (without any dielectric) is now filled with three dielectric slabs of dielectric constants $K_{1}=2,K_{2}=3$ and $K_{3}=5$ (as shown in figure). If new capacitance is $\frac{n}{3}C$ then the value of $n$ is $____$ .

[IMG]
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 23rd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor without any dielectric is given by:

$C=\frac{𝜖_{0}A}{d}$

where A is the area of the plates and d is the separation between them.


[IMG]


Capacitor $\mathrm{C}_{1}$

Dielectric constant $\mathrm{K}_{1}=2$.

Thickness $\mathrm{d}_{1}=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{2}$.

Area $\mathrm{A}_{1}=\mathrm{A}$

So, the capacitance is;

$C_{1}=\frac{K_{1}𝜖_{0}A_{1}}{d_{1}}=\frac{2𝜖_{0}A}{d/2}=4\left (\frac{𝜖_{0}A}{d}\right )=4C$

Capacitor $\mathrm{C}_{2}$

Dielectric constant $\mathrm{K}_{2}=3$.

Thickness $\mathrm{d}_{2}=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{2}$.

Area $\mathrm{A}_{2}=\mathrm{A}/2$

So, the capacitance is;

$\mathrm{C}_{2}=\frac{\mathrm{K}_{2}𝜖_{0}\mathrm{A}_{2}}{\mathrm{d}_{2}}=\frac{3𝜖_{0}(\mathrm{A}/2)}{\mathrm{d}/2}=3\left (\frac{𝜖_{0}\mathrm{A}}{\mathrm{d}}\right )=3\mathrm{C}$

Capacitor $\mathrm{C}_{3}$

Dielectric constant $\mathrm{K}_{3}=5$.

Thickness $\mathrm{d}_{3}=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{2}$.

Area $\mathrm{A}_{3}=\mathrm{A}/2$

So, the capacitance is;

$\mathrm{C}_{3}=\frac{\mathrm{K}_{3}𝜖_{0}\mathrm{A}_{3}}{\mathrm{d}_{3}}=\frac{5𝜖_{0}(\mathrm{A}/2)}{\mathrm{d}/2}=5\left (\frac{𝜖_{0}\mathrm{A}}{\mathrm{d}}\right )=5\mathrm{C}$

Capacitors $C_{2}$ and $C_{3}$ are in parallel.

$C_{23}=C_{2}+C_{3}$

$\Rightarrow$ $C_{23}=3C+5C=8C$

This combined section $(\mathrm{C}_{23})$ is in series with the first capacitor $(\mathrm{C}_{1})$.

$\frac{1}{\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{eq}}}=\frac{1}{\mathrm{C}_{1}}+\frac{1}{\mathrm{C}_{23}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{1}{\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{eq}}}=\frac{1}{4\mathrm{C}}+\frac{1}{8\mathrm{C}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{1}{C_{\mathrm{eq}}}=\frac{2+1}{8C}=\frac{3}{8C}$

$\Rightarrow$ $C_{\mathrm{eq}}=\frac{8C}{3}=\frac{n}{3}C\Rightarrow n=8$

Therefore, the value of n is 8 . Hence, the correct answer is 8 .

The equation of the electric field of an electromagnetic wave propagating through free space is given by : $E=\sqrt{377}\sin \left (6.27\times 10^{3}t-2.09\times 10^{-5}x\right )\mathrm{N}/\mathrm{C}$

The average power of the electromagnetic wave is $\left (\frac{1}{α}\right )\mathrm{W}/\mathrm{m}^{2}$. The value of $α$ is $____$ .

$\left (\text{Take}\sqrt{\frac{μ_{0}}{ε_{o}}}=377\text{in SI units}\right )$
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 23rd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The standard wave equation for the electric field component of an electromagnetic wave is given as $\mathrm{E}=\mathrm{E}_{0}\sin (ω\mathrm{t}-\mathrm{kx})$, where $\mathrm{E}_{0}$ is the amplitude of electric field, $ω$ is the angular frequency and k is the wave number.

The given equation for the electric field of electromagnetic wave is $=\sqrt{377}\sin \left (6.27\times 10^{3}t-2.09\times 10^{-5}\mathrm{x}\right )\mathrm{N}/\mathrm{C}$

So, electric field amplitude is $\mathrm{E}_{0}=\sqrt{377}\mathrm{N}/\mathrm{C}$.

The total energy density (energy per unit volume) of an electromagnetic wave is the sum of the electric field energy density ( $\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{E}}$ ) and magnetic field energy density ( $\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{B}}$ ).

$\mathrm{u}=\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{E}}+\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{B}}=\frac{1}{2}𝜖_{0}\mathrm{E}^{2}+\frac{\mathrm{B}^{2}}{2μ_{0}}$

In an electromagnetic wave traveling in a vacuum, the instantaneous electric and magnetic fields are related by the speed of light (c):

$\mathrm{E}=\mathrm{cB}\Rightarrow \mathrm{B}=\frac{\mathrm{E}}{\mathrm{c}}$

So, the energy density for magnetic field is,

$u_{B}=\frac{1}{2μ_{0}}\left (\frac{E}{c}\right )^{2}=\frac{E^{2}}{2μ_{0}c^{2}}$

Since $c=\frac{1}{\sqrt{μ_{0}𝜖_{0}}}\Rightarrow c^{2}=\frac{1}{μ_{0}𝜖_{0}}\Rightarrow μ_{0}c^{2}=\frac{1}{𝜖_{0}}$.

$\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{B}}=\frac{1}{2}𝜖_{0}\mathrm{E}^{2}$

Thus, the energy is equally shared: $\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{E}}=\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{B}}$.

The total instantaneous energy density is:

$\mathrm{u}=\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{E}}+\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{B}}=\frac{1}{2}𝜖_{0}\mathrm{E}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}𝜖_{0}\mathrm{E}^{2}=𝜖_{0}\mathrm{E}^{2}$

Since the electric field oscillates sinusoidally $(E=E_{0}\sin ωt)$, the average value of $E^{2}$ over one cycle is $\frac{E_{0}^{2}}{2}$.

$\mathrm{u}–=𝜖_{0}\left (\frac{\mathrm{E}_{0}^{2}}{2}\right )=\frac{1}{2}𝜖_{0}\mathrm{E}_{0}^{2}$

Intensity is defined as the energy crossing a unit area per unit time. It is related to the average energy density by the speed of the wave $c$ :

$\mathrm{I}=\mathrm{u}–\times \mathrm{c}$

$\Rightarrow$ $I=\left (\frac{1}{2}𝜖_{0}E_{0}^{2}\right )c$

The characteristic impedance of free space, $\mathrm{Z}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{μ_{0}}{𝜖_{0}}}$ (approx $377\Omega$ ).

$I=\frac{1}{2}𝜖_{0}E_{0}^{2}\left (\frac{1}{\sqrt{μ_{0}𝜖_{0}}}\right )$

$\Rightarrow$ $I=\frac{E_{0}^{2}}{2}\left (\frac{𝜖_{0}}{\sqrt{μ_{0}𝜖_{0}}}\right )=\frac{E_{0}^{2}}{2}\sqrt{\frac{𝜖_{0}}{μ_{0}}}=\frac{(\sqrt{377})^{2}}{2}\times \frac{1}{377}=\frac{1}{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{α}\Rightarrow α=2$

Therefore, the value of $α$ is 2.

text: In two separate Young's double-slit experimental set-ups and two monochromatic light sources of different wavelengths are used to get fringes of equal width. The ratios of the slits separations and that of the wavelengths of light used are $2:1$ and $1:2$ respectively. The corresponding ratio of the distances between the slits and the respective screens ( $D_{1}/D_{2}$ ) is $____$。
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 23rd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
In two Young's Double Slit Experiments (YDSE) the fringe widths are equal ( $β_{1}=β_{2}$ ).

Ratio of slit separations (d) is $\frac{\mathrm{d}_{1}}{\mathrm{d}_{2}}=\frac{2}{1}=2$

Ratio of wavelengths ( $λ$ ) is $\frac{λ_{1}}{λ_{2}}=\frac{1}{2}$

The formula for fringe width ( $β$ ) in a YDSE setup is:

$β=\frac{λD}{d}$

where:

$λ$ is the wavelength of light.

D is the distance between the slits and the screen.

d is the separation between the slits.

$β_{1}=β_{2}\Rightarrow \frac{λ_{1}\mathrm{D}_{1}}{\mathrm{d}_{1}}=\frac{λ_{2}\mathrm{D}_{2}}{\mathrm{d}_{2}}$

$\Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{D}_{1}}{\mathrm{D}_{2}}=\left (\frac{λ_{2}}{λ_{1}}\right )\times \left (\frac{\mathrm{d}_{1}}{\mathrm{d}_{2}}\right )$

Since $\frac{λ_{1}}{λ_{2}}=\frac{1}{2}$, so, $\frac{λ_{2}}{λ_{1}}=2$

Putting the values into the equation :

$\frac{\mathrm{D}_{1}}{\mathrm{D}_{2}}=(2)\times (2)=4$

The corresponding ratio of the distances between the slits and the respective screens is $4:1$. 

Hence, the correct answer is $𝟒$.

Using a variable frequency a.c. voltage source the maximum current measured in the given LCR circuit is 50 mA for $V=5\sin (100t)$ The values of $L$ and $R$ are shown in the figure. The capacitance of the capacitor ( C ) used is $____$ $μ\mathrm{F}$.


[IMG]
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 23rd January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
In a series LCR circuit, the current reaches its maximum value when the circuit is at resonance.

At resonance the inductive reactance $(X_{L})$ equals the capacitive reactance $(X_{C})$.

The total impedance $(\mathrm{Z})$ is $\mathrm{Z}=\sqrt{\mathrm{R}^{2}+(\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{L}}-\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{C}})^{2}}=\mathrm{R}$, purely resistive and minimum.

So, the peak current is given by $\mathrm{I}_{0}=\frac{\mathrm{V}_{0}}{\mathrm{Z}}=\frac{\mathrm{V}_{0}}{\mathrm{R}}$.

From the given equation of a.c. voltage is $\mathrm{V}=5\sin (100\mathrm{t})$. So, the peak voltage is $\mathrm{V}_{0}=5\mathrm{V}$

The resistance is $\mathrm{R}=100\Omega =\mathrm{Z}$.

So, the calculated value of peak current is

$\mathrm{I}_{0}=\frac{5}{100}=0.05\mathrm{A}=50\mathrm{mA}.$

This shows that the circuit is in resonance state.

From the voltage equation $\mathrm{V}=5\sin (100\mathrm{t})$,

$ω=100\mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}$

Using the resonance condition $\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{L}}=\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{C}}$ :

$ωL=\frac{1}{ωC}$

$\Rightarrow$ $C=\frac{1}{ω^{2}L}$

Putting the values, we get

$C=\frac{1}{(100)^{2}\times 2}=\frac{1}{20000}F=\frac{10^{6}}{20000}μF=50μF$

Therefore, the capacitance of the capacitor is $50μ\mathrm{F}$. Hence, the correct answer is 50.
